diagnostic_evidence.quote: with the core tensor $\boldsymbol{\beta}^0$ and  the orthogonal Tucker factor matrices $V^{(\ell)} G^{(\ell)} \in \R^{n_\ell \times r_\ell^0}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof justifies orthogonality of the factor matrices by asserting $V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}[G^{(\ell)}]^T[V^{(\ell)}]^T=I_{n_\ell}$. Since $V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}\in\R^{n_\ell\times r_\ell^0}$, the left-hand side is an orthogonal projection of rank $r_\ell^0$ and cannot equal $I_{n_\ell}$ unless $r_\ell^0=n_\ell$, contradicting the small-rank setting ($|{\bf r}_0|<|{\bf r}|\le n_\ell$). The correct identity is $[G^{(\ell)}]^T[V^{(\ell)}]^TV^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}=I_{r_\ell^0}$, which does yield the proposition's conclusion; as written the proof's key step is false.

failure_location.quote: proves the orthogonality  $V^{(\ell)} G^{(\ell)} [G^{(\ell)}]^T [V^{(\ell)}]^T =I_{n_\ell}$, which completes the proof.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the asserted identity by the column-orthogonality relation $[G^{(\ell)}]^T[V^{(\ell)}]^TV^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}=I_{r_\ell^0}$, using orthonormal columns of $V^{(\ell)}$ and $G^{(\ell)}$.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Proposition hybrid2Tuck is invalid as written. Its conclusion (conversion of the two-level Tucker format to a rank-${\bf r}^0$ Tucker format with orthogonal factors) remains true, and no later result builds on the false identity.

issues.failure_explanation: The claim that $T_{0:m_\ell-1}(x_\ell)V^{(\ell)}$ are orthogonal polynomials when $V^{(\ell)}$ has orthonormal columns is false under the natural Chebyshev-weighted inner product: $\|T_0\|_w=\sqrt2\,\|T_k\|_w$ for $k\ge1$, so e.g. orthonormal columns $V=\frac1{\sqrt2}\binom{1\;\;1}{1\;-1}$ give polynomials $(1\pm x)/\sqrt2$ with weighted inner product $\pi/4\ne0$. The proof only remarks that 'the inner product should be properly weighted' and gives no argument. The stated cardinality $r_\ell^0$ also mismatches the $r_\ell$ entries of $T_{0:m_\ell-1}V^{(\ell)}$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: It enjoys strong theoretical guarantees such that for any given $\varepsilon > 0$, it can approximate the original tensor in the sense of relative error $\|{\bf C} - \hat{\bf C}\|_{\mathrm{F}} \leq \varepsilon\|{\bf C}\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ with almost optimal rank parameters
We use the classical Tucker-ALS algorithm in our theoretical analysis and numerical experiments

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's final step presumes the Tucker-ALS output satisfies $\|{\bf C}-\hat{\bf C}\|_F\le\varepsilon\|{\bf C}\|_F$, where $\varepsilon$ is the user tolerance of tuck\_als. The only support is the remark's claim that Tucker-ALS 'enjoys strong theoretical guarantees' of exactly this kind with almost optimal ranks. ALS/HOOI is a nonconvex alternating iteration with only local convergence properties; the cited works concern the best multilinear-rank approximation, not that ALS attains a prescribed relative error at near-optimal ranks. The premise is therefore unestablished, and the stated bound on Algorithm 1's output in terms of the input tolerance $\varepsilon$ is unproven.

failure_location.quote: where we also used the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the relative truncation error $\varepsilon$ of the Tucker approximation in the last line.

issues.overall_effect: The guaranteed-accuracy statement for the functional-case ChebTuck approximation (Proposition cheb_tuck_error, and the 'controllable accuracy' claim for Algorithms 1-3) is conditional on an unverified algorithmic property.

issues.failure_explanation: Both the statement and the proof use the CP weights $\xi_k\in\mathbb R$ without absolute values; the step $|\sum_k\xi_k(\cdot)|\le\sum_k\xi_k|\cdot|$ is invalid for negative $\xi_k$, and the first stated bound then fails (e.g. $R=1$, $\xi_1=-1$ gives a negative right-hand side). Since the paper's setting permits real weights (charges $z_v\in\mathbb R$; CP weights after tensor transforms may be negative), the lemma as stated is false; the valid form requires $|\xi_k|$ (the second bound with $\|\boldsymbol\xi\|_1=\sum|\xi_k|$ is the correct one).

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where ${\bf a}_k^{(\ell)} \in \R^{n_\ell}$ are $\ell_2$ normalized canonical vectors of each mode
the singular values $\sigma_k^{(\ell)}$ are available after the SVD decomposition of the side matrices in the CP format

issues.failure_explanation: The bound is obtained by invoking the cited RHOSVD truncation theorem on ${\bf C}=\sum_k\xi_k{\bf c}_k^{(1)}\otimes{\bf c}_k^{(2)}\otimes{\bf c}_k^{(3)}$. The singular values $\sigma_k^{(\ell)}$ are never defined in the paper, and the canonical vectors ${\bf c}_k^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}{\bf q}_k^{(\ell)}$ are not normalized (only the input vectors ${\bf a}_k^{(\ell)}$ are $\ell_2$-normalized; spline sampling and the DCT change norms, e.g. from $\approx1/\sqrt n$ to $\approx\sqrt2$). Bounds of the stated form, with the bare factor $\|\boldsymbol\xi\|_2$ and side-matrix singular values, are valid only for unit-norm canonical vectors; for unnormalized vectors they can fail: with $R=1$ and mode 1 truncated to rank 0, the error is $|\xi_1|\prod_\ell\|{\bf c}^{(\ell)}\|$ while the bound gives $|\xi_1|\|{\bf c}^{(1)}\|$, which is violated whenever $\|{\bf c}^{(2)}\|\|{\bf c}^{(3)}\|>1$. The proof therefore does not establish the lemma, and Theorem added-1's second term inherits the gap.

failure_location.quote: The desired result then follows from the standard error analysis of the RHOSVD truncation \cite[Theorem 2.5]{khoromskij2009multigrid}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Renormalize the CP representation of ${\bf C}$ (absorb $\|{\bf c}_k^{(\ell)}\|$ into modified weights $\tilde\xi_k=\xi_k\prod_\ell\|{\bf c}_k^{(\ell)}\|$), define $\sigma_k^{(\ell)}$ explicitly as the singular values of the side matrices in the form required by the cited theorem, and restate the lemma and Theorem added-1 with $\|\tilde{\boldsymbol\xi}\|_2$.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma ftilde-fhat and the RHOSVD part of Theorem added-1 (the a priori error bound for the CP-input Algorithm 4, the paper's preferred algorithm) are unproven as stated and can fail by data-dependent factors; the adaptive rank-selection scheme proposed in the following remark inherits this.
issues.title: RHOSVD error bound applied to unnormalized canonical vectors with undefined singular values
issues.why_classification: A contained but nontrivial restatement (renormalization, redefinition of the singular values and of the weight norm, and adjustment of the theorem) is required; the bound's structure survives but the stated constants are not correct as written.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \cref{alg:cheb_tuck_alg}: $C_4 m^3(m+n) + C_5 m^3 + C_1 m^3 \log m + C_2 m^4 + C_3 m^4 |\log \varepsilon|$.
Given a tensor ${\bf F}\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3}$ discretizing function $f: [-1,1]^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ on the uniform grid

issues.failure_explanation: The 'similarly' inference from the univariate cost $O(m+n)$ to a trivariate cost $O(m^3(m+n))$ is invalid. Constructing the trivariate spline of the $n^3$ data (tridiagonal solves along all grid lines, as in MATLAB interpn) already costs $\Theta(n^3)$, and mode-by-mode evaluation at the $m^3$ Chebyshev points costs $O((m+n)(n^2+mn+m^2))$; the input itself has $n^3$ entries. In the paper's regime $m\ll n$ (e.g. $m=129$, $n=2048$) the claimed bound $m^3(m+n)$ is smaller than these unavoidable costs, so the stated complexity estimate for Algorithm 2 is not a valid upper bound.

failure_location.quote: Similarly, the cost of trivariate cubic spline interpolation which is required in \cref{alg:cheb_tuck_alg} is $\mathcal{O}(m^3(m+n))$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the $C_4m^3(m+n)$ term by the correct spline-related cost, e.g. $O(n^3+m^3)$ (or $O((m+n)(m^2+mn+n^2))$ for mode-by-mode evaluation), in the Algorithm 2 estimate.
issues.overall_effect: The Algorithm 2 line of Proposition compl is unreliable. The qualitative narrative (Algorithm 2 is the expensive full-grid baseline) survives, and no other formal result uses this bound.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \cref{alg:cheb_tuck_func}: $C_{f} m^3 + C_1 m^3 \log m + C_2 m^4 + C_3 m^4 |\log \varepsilon|$.
\cref{alg:cheb_tuck_alg_cp_2}: $C_6 nR + C_7 mR + C_9 m R\log m + C_{10} mR \min\{m,R\} + C_{11} R |\log \varepsilon|^3$.

issues.failure_explanation: The $\varepsilon$-dependent terms of all four complexity estimates ($C_3m^4|\log\varepsilon|$, $C_{11}R|\log\varepsilon|^3$) are obtained by substituting $r=O(|\log\varepsilon|)$ for the Tucker/RHOSVD ranks. This rank-tolerance relation is a data-dependent spectral property (it fails, e.g., for inputs whose side matrices have slowly decaying singular values, where ranks up to $\min\{m,R\}$ are needed), yet it appears in none of the proposition's hypotheses, which are stated for general $f$ or general CP input. The proof merely says the relation 'is assumed' and asserts it holds for 'a wide range of functions', citing a result on grid-based canonical tensors of the Newton kernel, which does not establish the claim for the Chebyshev coefficient tensors treated here.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: {\bf P}_{R_s} = \sum_{k=1}^{R_s} {\bf p}_k \otimes {\bf p}_k \otimes {\bf p}_k, \quad {\bf P}_{R_l} = \sum_{k=R_s+1}^{R} {\bf p}_k \otimes {\bf p}_k \otimes {\bf p}_k.

We can see that canonical vectors representing the long-range behavior of the Newton kernel, i.e., ${\bf p}_1, \cdots, {\bf p}_{15}$ can be well approximated by low-degree Chebyshev interpolants (left), while for short-range canonical vectors, the convergence is much slower (middle).
if we separate the long-range part of the potential by taking out the last $22$ canonical vectors, the error is reduced to the magnitude $10^{-6}$

issues.failure_explanation: Equation eqn:Split_Tens defines the short-range part as the head sum ${\bf P}_{R_s}=\sum_{k\le R_s}$ and the long-range part as the tail sum ${\bf P}_{R_l}=\sum_{k>R_s}$, and the prose calls ${\bf P}_{R_s}$ 'highly localized'. The paper's own measurements on the same canonical vectors show the opposite ordering: ${\bf p}_1,\dots,{\bf p}_{15}$ are the smooth, slowly decaying (long-range) vectors, while the large-index vectors are the localized (short-range) ones with a 'jump around k=15'; the lattice discussion likewise obtains the long-range part by removing the last vectors; and tab:lr_single_newton_error shows ${\bf P}_{R_l}$ is well approximated at small $m$, possible only if it consists of the smooth small-index vectors. As written, the splitting assigns the labels backwards: following it literally would treat the smooth head sum as the localized short-range part and apply ChebTuck to the spiky tail, contradicting the paper's own figures, tables, and usage.

failure_location.quote: Then the short-range part ${\bf P}_{R_s}$ is a highly localized tensor which has very small support and can thus be stored sparsely (see \cite{benner2018range} for details), while the ChebTuck approximation can be gainfully applied to the long-range part ${\bf P}_{R_l}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Swap the index ranges (or the labels) in eqn:Split_Tens so that the localized short-range part is the sum over large $k$ and the long-range part is the head sum, matching the paper's own figures and numerical usage.
issues.overall_effect: The definition of the short- and long-range components in Section 4.1.3 is internally inconsistent with the paper's figures, error tables, and lattice discussion; an implementation following this equation would split the tensor the wrong way.
issues.title: Short-/long-range index ranges in the range-separation splitting contradict the paper's own data
issues.why_classification: A local relabeling restores consistency; all numerical results and the method itself are consistent with the corrected reading, and no labelled formal result depends on the equation.
